claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of action potential amplitude and half-duration before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: HCN channels do not alter the active membrane properties of cerebellar mossy fiber boutons profoundly.
claims.source: In both cases, the amplitude and half-duration of the action potentials elicited at 1 Hz were not significantly affected by the application of 30 µM ZD7288 (data not shown and Figure 4B and C, respectively), indicating that HCN channels do not alter the active membrane properties profoundly.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ZD7288 does not significantly affect action potential amplitude and half-duration at 1 Hz.

claims.claim: Blocking HCN channels significantly impaired the ability of mossy fibers to fire at high frequencies.
claims.source: Blocking HCN channels significantly impaired the ability of mossy fibers to fire at high frequencies (20 stimuli at 200–1666 Hz).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced failure-free firing frequency in the presence of ZD7288, as shown in Figure 4D-E.

claims.claim: The average failure-free frequency in cerebellar mossy fibers was reduced from 854 ± 60 Hz under control conditions to 426 ± 63 Hz in the presence of ZD7288 (n = 20 and 10, respectively; PT-Test = 0.0002).
claims.source: The average failure-free frequency was reduced from 854 ± 60 Hz under control conditions to 426 ± 63 Hz in the presence of ZD7288 (n = 20 and 10, respectively; PT-Test = 0.0002; Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of failure-free firing frequency in cMFBs before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: HCN channels ensure reliable high-frequency firing in cerebellar mossy fibers.
claims.source: These experiments show, that HCNs, despite their slow kinetics, ensure reliable high-frequency firing.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that blocking HCN channels reduces the maximal failure-free firing frequency and increases action potential failures during high-frequency trains.

claims.claim: ZD7288 caused a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons (–80.0 ± 0.6 mV and –85.4 ± 1.4 mV for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs, n = 94 and 35, respectively).
claims.source: ZD7288 caused (i) a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV (–80.0 ± 0.6 mV and –85.4 ± 1.4 mV for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs n = 94 and 35, respectively), (ii) a doubling of the apparent input resistance calculated from the steady-state voltage at the end of the current step (794 ± 48 MΩ and 1681 ± 185 MΩ, respectively), and (iii) a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant, as determined by a mono-exponential fit to the initial decay of the membrane potential (14.4 ± 0.8 ms and 35.0 ± 2.5 ms, respectively; see legend of Figure 5B for statistical testing).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of resting membrane potential in cMFBs before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: ZD7288 caused a doubling of the apparent input resistance in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons (794 ± 48 MΩ and 1681 ± 185 MΩ for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs, respectively).
claims.source: ZD7288 caused (i) a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV (–80.0 ± 0.6 mV and –85.4 ± 1.4 mV for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs n = 94 and 35, respectively), (ii) a doubling of the apparent input resistance calculated from the steady-state voltage at the end of the current step (794 ± 48 MΩ and 1681 ± 185 MΩ, respectively), and (iii) a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant, as determined by a mono-exponential fit to the initial decay of the membrane potential (14.4 ± 0.8 ms and 35.0 ± 2.5 ms, respectively; see legend of Figure 5B for statistical testing).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of apparent input resistance in cMFBs before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: ZD7288 caused a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons (14.4 ± 0.8 ms and 35.0 ± 2.5 ms for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs, respectively).
claims.source: ZD7288 caused (i) a hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential by, on average, 5.4 mV (–80.0 ± 0.6 mV and –85.4 ± 1.4 mV for control and ZD7288-treated cMFBs n = 94 and 35, respectively), (ii) a doubling of the apparent input resistance calculated from the steady-state voltage at the end of the current step (794 ± 48 MΩ and 1681 ± 185 MΩ, respectively), and (iii) a doubling of the apparent membrane time constant, as determined by a mono-exponential fit to the initial decay of the membrane potential (14.4 ± 0.8 ms and 35.0 ± 2.5 ms, respectively; see legend of Figure 5B for statistical testing).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of apparent membrane time constant in cMFBs before and after ZD7288 application, as shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Adding cAMP in various concentrations to the intracellular solution depolarized the membrane potential and decreased both the input resistance and the apparent membrane time constant in a concentration-dependent manner in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: Adding cAMP in various concentrations to the intracellular solution depolarized the membrane potential and decreased both the input resistance and the apparent membrane time constant in a concentration-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of membrane potential, input resistance, and membrane time constant with different intracellular cAMP concentrations, as shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: HCN channels in cerebellar mossy fibers determine the passive membrane properties as a function of the intracellular cAMP concentration.
claims.source: These data suggest that HCN channels in cerebellar mossy fibers determine the passive membrane properties as a function of the intracellular cAMP concentration.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both ZD7288 and varying intracellular cAMP concentrations affect passive membrane properties in opposite directions.

claims.claim: HCN2 is the dominating subunit in cerebellar mossy fibers.
claims.source: In addition, immunogold-electron microscopy revealed HCN2 as the dominating subunit in cerebellar mossy fibers.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy showing significant labeling for HCN2 but only background immunoreactivity for HCN1 in cMFBs, as shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Immunogold labeling revealed only background immunoreactivity for HCN1 in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: At the electron microscopic level, we found only background immunoreactivity for HCN1 (data not shown) but significant labeling for HCN2 (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy showing no significant HCN1 labeling in cMFBs.

claims.claim: Immunogold labeling revealed significant labeling for HCN2 in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: At the electron microscopic level, we found only background immunoreactivity for HCN1 (data not shown) but significant labeling for HCN2 (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy showing significant HCN2 labeling in cMFBs, as shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: HCN2 immunogold particles were diffusely distributed along the plasma membrane of cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, with similar labeling density in the adjacent mossy fiber axon.
claims.source: HCN2 immunogold particles were diffusely distributed along the plasma membrane of cMFBs, with similar labeling density in the adjacent mossy fiber axon (Figure 6B), which could be traced back up to 3.5 µm from cMFBs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunogold electron microscopy showing diffuse distribution of HCN2 particles along the plasma membrane of cMFBs and adjacent axons, as shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: HCN2 was uniformly distributed without apparent spatial relations to synapses in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: HCN2 was uniformly distributed without apparent spatial relations to those synapses.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 3D reconstruction of a cMFB showing uniform distribution of HCN2 gold particles without spatial clustering near synapses, as shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The density of immunogold particles for HCN2 in a reconstructed cerebellar mossy fiber bouton was 17.1 particles/µm2 (in total 1260 particles per 73.65 µm2).
claims.source: The density of immunogold particles for HCN2 in this reconstructed bouton was 17.1 particles/µm2 (in total 1260 particles per 73.65 µm2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunogold particles in a 3D reconstructed cMFB.

claims.claim: The mean density of immunogold particles for HCN2 in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was 22.7 ± 2.4 per μm2 (n = 6 cMFBs from two mice).
claims.source: The mean density of immunogold particles for HCN2 was 22.7 ± 2.4 per μm2 (n = 6 cMFBs from two mice).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunogold particles across multiple cMFBs.

claims.claim: HCN2 is the dominant subunit mediating Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, consistent with its pronounced cAMP-dependence.
claims.source: These data indicate that HCN2 is the dominant subunit mediating Ih in cMFBs, consistent with its pronounced cAMP-dependence.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from immunogold labeling showing predominant HCN2 expression and the observed strong cAMP-dependence of Ih in cMFBs.

claims.claim: Hyperpolarizing voltage steps evoked a slowly activating, non-inactivating inward current in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons, which was inhibited by ZD7288.
claims.source: Hyperpolarizing voltage steps evoked a slowly activating, non-inactivating inward current, which was inhibited by ZD7288 (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings from cMFBs showing slowly activating, non-inactivating inward currents that are blocked by ZD7288, as shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The mean V½ of Ih activation in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was –103.3 ± 0.8 mV (n = 36).
claims.source: Using the tail currents of ZD7288-sensitive currents evoked by voltage steps between –80 mV and –150 mV from a holding potential of –70 mV, we calculated the activation curve of Ih with a mean V½ of –103.3 ± 0.8 mV (Figure 7B; n = 36 V½-values, each from a different cMFB).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of tail currents from voltage-clamp recordings in cMFBs, as shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: About 7% of the overall HCN2-mediated current is active at rest in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
claims.source: On the basis of the average resting membrane potential of cMFBs, this means that about 7% of the overall HCN2-mediated current is active at rest.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the V½ of Ih activation and the average resting membrane potential of cMFBs.

claims.claim: With 1 mM cAMP, V½ of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons shifted by 17 mV to, on average, –86.6 ± 1.2 mV (n = 16 cMFBs; PT-Test <10−10).
claims.source: With 1 mM cAMP, V½ shifted by 17 mV to, on average, –86.6 ± 1.2 mV (n = 16 cMFBs; PT-Test <10−10; Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings from cMFBs with 1 mM cAMP in the intracellular solution, as shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The EC50 of intracellular cAMP for the shift in V½ of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons is 40.4 µM.
claims.source: The resulting average shifts of V½ revealed an EC50 of 40.4 µM intracellular cAMP (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of V½ shifts at different intracellular cAMP concentrations, as shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Under perforated patch conditions, the V½ of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was –96.4 ± 1.2 mV (n = 10), significantly more depolarized than the corresponding whole-cell recordings after rupture of the perforated patch (–101.3 ± 1.0 mV; n = 10; PT-Test = 0.0076).
claims.source: Under perforated patch conditions, the V½ of Ih was –96.4 ± 1.2 mV (n = 10), significantly more depolarized than the corresponding whole-cell recordings after rupture of the perforated patch (–101.3 ± 1.0 mV; n = 10; PT-Test = 0.0076; Figure 7C; see Materials and methods for comparisons with additional control groups).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by perforated patch recordings from cMFBs compared to whole-cell recordings, as shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The endogenous cAMP concentration in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons is 12.6 µM, with a 68% confidence interval of 1.8 to 60.7 µM cAMP.
claims.source: This voltage shift (4.9 ± 1.2 mV, n = 10 cMFBs) indicates an endogenous cAMP concentration of 12.6 µM in cMFBs, with a 68% confidence interval of 1.8 to 60.7 µM cAMP (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the voltage shift observed in perforated patch recordings and the EC50 of cAMP for Ih activation, as shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The reversal potential of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons was –23.4 ± 1.4 mV (n = 7).
claims.source: Furthermore, we estimated the reversal potential of Ih with short voltage ramps as described previously (Cuttle et al., 2001) and found a value of –23.4 ± 1.4 mV (n = 7; Figure 8C), similar to previous estimates (Aponte et al., 2006; Cuttle et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurements using voltage ramps in cMFBs, as shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: The depolarization caused by HCN2 channels controls conduction velocity in cerebellar mossy fibers.
claims.source: The results showed that the Vm-model but not the Rm-model caused an increase in conduction velocity, indicating that the depolarizing effect of axonal HCN2 channels determines conduction velocity (Figure 9E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing that only the model simulating depolarization (Vm-model) but not the model simulating decreased membrane resistance (Rm-model) increased conduction velocity, as shown in Figure 9E.

claims.claim: Increasing the resting membrane potential from –90 mV to –65 mV decreased the availability of voltage-dependent Na+ channels but increased the conduction velocity in the computational model.
claims.source: Interestingly, increasing the resting membrane potential from –90 mV to –65 mV, decreased the availability of voltage-dependent Na+ (NaV) channels but increased the conduction velocity (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing that depolarization increases conduction velocity despite decreasing Na+ channel availability, as shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The conduction velocity decreased only at resting membrane potentials above –65 mV in the computational model.
claims.source: The conduction velocity decreased only at resting membrane potentials above –65 mV in our model.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing a non-linear relationship between resting membrane potential and conduction velocity, as shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The depolarization mediated by HCN2 channels accelerates the conduction velocity by bringing the membrane potential closer to the firing threshold.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that the depolarization mediated by HCN2 channels accelerates the conduction velocity by bringing the membrane potential closer to the firing threshold.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from computational modeling showing that depolarization, not decreased membrane resistance, increases conduction velocity.

claims.claim: It is approximately 100% more expensive to maintain the resting membrane potential with Ih than without or by depolarization alone in the computational model.
claims.source: Computational modeling showed that it is ~100% more expensive to maintain the resting membrane potential with Ih than without or by depolarization alone (Vm-model; Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling of ATP consumption required to maintain the resting membrane potential, as shown in Figure 9F.

claims.claim: The metabolic cost of maintaining the resting membrane potential with Ih for one second was approximately 3-fold higher than the cost of generating one action potential in the computational model.
claims.source: Furthermore, the metabolic cost of maintaining the resting membrane potential with Ih for one second was ~3-fold higher than the cost of generating one action potential (Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling of ATP consumption for maintaining resting potential versus generating action potentials, as shown in Figure 9F.

claims.claim: Assuming an average frequency of cerebellar mossy fibers of 4 Hz in vivo, the HCN2 channels increased the required energy of cerebellar mossy fibers by approximately 30%.
claims.source: Assuming an average frequency of cerebellar mossy fibers of 4 Hz in vivo (Chadderton et al., 2004; Rancz et al., 2007), the HCN2 channels increased the required energy of cerebellar mossy fibers by ~30%.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from computational modeling of ATP consumption and literature values for average firing frequency in vivo.

claims.claim: HCN channels are a major consumer of the energetic demands of axons.
claims.source: These data indicate that HCN2 channels are a major consumer of the energetic demands of axons.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from computational modeling showing high metabolic costs of HCN channels for maintaining resting membrane potential.

claims.claim: HCN channels increase action potential velocity and fidelity in central axons.
claims.source: Here, we demonstrate that the HCN channels increase action potential velocity and fidelity in central axons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that HCN channels increase conduction velocity and ensure reliable high-frequency firing.

claims.claim: HCN channels control conduction velocity primarily by altering the resting membrane potential.
claims.source: Computational modeling indicated that HCN2 channels control conduction velocity primarily by altering the resting membrane potential and are associated with significant metabolic costs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing that the Vm-model but not the Rm-model reproduces the effects of HCN channels on conduction velocity.

claims.claim: HCN channels are associated with significant metabolic costs.
claims.source: Computational modeling indicated that HCN2 channels control conduction velocity primarily by altering the resting membrane potential and are associated with significant metabolic costs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing high ATP consumption for maintaining resting membrane potential with HCN channels.

claims.claim: The cAMP-HCN pathway provides neuromodulators with an opportunity to finely tune energy consumption and temporal delays across axons in the brain.
claims.source: These results suggest that the cAMP-HCN pathway provides neuromodulators with an opportunity to finely tune energy consumption and temporal delays across axons in the brain.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing neuromodulator effects on conduction velocity and computational modeling showing metabolic costs of HCN channels.

claims.claim: HCN channels are expressed in the heart and nervous system and comprise four members (HCN1–HCN4).
claims.source: HCN channels are expressed in the heart and nervous system and comprise four members (HCN1–HCN4), which differ in their kinetics, voltage-dependence and degree of sensitivity to cyclic nucleotides such as cAMP (Biel et al., 2009; Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: HCN1–HCN4 differ in their kinetics, voltage-dependence and degree of sensitivity to cyclic nucleotides such as cAMP.
claims.source: HCN channels are expressed in the heart and nervous system and comprise four members (HCN1–HCN4), which differ in their kinetics, voltage-dependence and degree of sensitivity to cyclic nucleotides such as cAMP (Biel et al., 2009; Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Membrane hyperpolarization activates HCN channels and causes a depolarizing mixed sodium/potassium (Na+/K+) current.
claims.source: Membrane hyperpolarization activates HCN channels and causes a depolarizing mixed sodium/potassium (Na+/K+) current.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about HCN channel function.

claims.claim: In the heart, the current through HCN channels (If) mediates the acceleratory effect of adrenaline on heart rate by direct binding of cAMP.
claims.source: In the heart, the current through HCN channels (If) mediates the acceleratory effect of adrenaline on heart rate by direct binding of cAMP (DiFrancesco, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: In neurons, the current through HCN channels (Ih) controls a wide array of functions, such as rhythmic activity and excitability.
claims.source: In neurons, the current through HCN channels (Ih) controls a wide array of functions, such as rhythmic activity (Pape and McCormick, 1989) and excitability (Tang and Trussell, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: HCN channels are expressed throughout various subcellular compartments of neurons.
claims.source: In addition to the somatic impact, HCN channels are expressed throughout various subcellular compartments of neurons (Nusser, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Patch-clamp recordings from dendrites in pyramidal neurons have revealed particularly high densities of HCN channels that act to control the local resting potential and leak conductance.
claims.source: For example, patch-clamp recordings from dendrites in pyramidal neurons have revealed particularly high densities of HCN channels that act to control the local resting potential and leak conductance, thereby playing important roles in regulating synaptic integration (George et al., 2009; Harnett et al., 2015; Kole et al., 2006; Magee, 1999; Williams and Stuart, 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Ih seems to control the strength of synaptic transmission in the crayfish and the Drosophila neuromuscular junction.
claims.source: Ih seems to control the strength of synaptic transmission in the crayfish and the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (Beaumont and Zucker, 2000; Cheung et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Presynaptic recordings from the vertebrate calyx of Held in the auditory brainstem found Ih to only have a marginal effect on neurotransmitter release.
claims.source: However, presynaptic recordings from the vertebrate calyx of Held in the auditory brainstem found Ih to only have a marginal effect on neurotransmitter release (Cuttle et al., 2001), but to exert a strong influence on the resting membrane potential (Cuttle et al., 2001; Kim and von Gersdorff, 2012) and on vesicular neurotransmitter uptake (Huang and Trussell, 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: At the synaptic terminals of pyramidal neurons in the cortex of mice, HCN channels inhibit glutamate release by suppressing the activity of T-type Ca2+ channels.
claims.source: At the synaptic terminals of pyramidal neurons in the cortex of mice, HCN channels inhibit glutamate release by suppressing the activity of T-type Ca2+ channels (Huang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: In axons of the stomatogastric nervous system of lobsters, the action potential conduction was affected by dopamine acting via axonal HCN channels.
claims.source: Indeed, in axons of the stomatogastric nervous system of lobsters (Marder and Bucher, 2001), the action potential conduction was affected by dopamine acting via axonal HCN channels (Ballo et al., 2010; Ballo et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Studies on action potential propagation by Waxman and coworkers indicated that Ih counteracts the hyperpolarization of the membrane potential during periods of high-frequency firing.
claims.source: In vertebrates, studies on action potential propagation by Waxman and coworkers indicated that Ih counteracts the hyperpolarization of the membrane potential during periods of high-frequency firing (Baker et al., 1987; Birch et al., 1991; Waxman et al., 1995), and that it participates in ionic homeostasis at the node of Ranvier (Waxman and Ritchie, 1993).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Ih is crucial for the emergence of persistent action potential firing in axons of parvalbumin-positive interneurons.
claims.source: More recent investigations found Ih to be crucial for the emergence of persistent action potential firing in axons of parvalbumin-positive interneurons (Elgueta et al., 2015), but Ih seems to have an opposing effect on the excitability at the axon initial segment, where its activation reduces the probability of action potential initiation (Ko et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: There is evidence from extracellular recordings that blocking Ih decreases the action potential conduction velocity in unmyelinated central axons and peripheral axons of vertebrates.
claims.source: Finally, there is evidence from extracellular recordings that blocking Ih decreases the action potential conduction velocity in unmyelinated central axons (Baginskas et al., 2009; Soleng et al., 2003) and peripheral axons of vertebrates (Grafe et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The neuromodulation of conduction velocity and the underlying cellular membrane mechanisms are not known in vertebrate axons.
claims.source: However, the neuromodulation of conduction velocity and the underlying cellular membrane mechanisms are not known in vertebrate axons.
claims.evidence: The claim identifies a gap in knowledge based on the absence of prior studies.

claims.claim: Cerebellar mossy fibers can conduct trains of action potentials at frequencies exceeding 1 kHz.
claims.source: However, cerebellar mossy fibers can conduct trains of action potentials at frequencies exceeding 1 kHz (Ritzau-Jost et al., 2014), making them an ideal target to investigate the impact of axonal HCNs on the propagation of high-frequency action potentials.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: HCN1 and HCN2 are predominantly expressed in the cerebellar cortex.
claims.source: Of the four HCN subunits (HCN1–HCN4), the subunits HCN1 and HCN2 are predominantly expressed in the cerebellar cortex (Notomi and Shigemoto, 2004; Santoro et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Previous studies in the cortex, hippocampus, and auditory brainstem primarily detected HCN1 in axons.
claims.source: Previous studies in the cortex, hippocampus, and auditory brainstem primarily detected HCN1 in axons (Elgueta et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2016), but HCN2 was found to be more sensitive to cAMP than HCN1 (Wang et al., 2001; Zagotta et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: HCN2 was found to be more sensitive to cAMP than HCN1.
claims.source: Previous studies in the cortex, hippocampus, and auditory brainstem primarily detected HCN1 in axons (Elgueta et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2016), but HCN2 was found to be more sensitive to cAMP than HCN1 (Wang et al., 2001; Zagotta et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The changes in baseline conduction velocity mediated by HCN channels are relatively small, in the range of approximately 5%.
claims.source: We describe both an increase and decrease of the baseline axonal conduction velocity in the range of ~5% mediated by HCN channels (Figures 1–3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Figures 1-3.

claims.claim: HCN channels can be expected to change the arrival time of the action potential by, for example, 0.5 ms in the case of unmyelinated cerebellar parallel fibers (assuming 3 mm length and 0.3 m/s velocity).
claims.source: Although the changes in baseline conduction velocity are relatively small, considering the long distances that axons traverse in the brain, HCN channels can be expected to change the arrival time of the action potential by, for example, 0.5 ms in the case of unmyelinated cerebellar parallel fibers (assuming 3 mm length and 0.3 m/s velocity; Swadlow and Waxman, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data on conduction velocity changes and literature values for axon length and velocity.

claims.claim: Temporal delays caused by HCN channels will influence information processing in the central nervous system, because spike-timing dependent plasticity, coincidence detection, and the neuronal rhythms of cell ensembles precisely tune the arrival times of action potentials.
claims.source: Such temporal delays will influence information processing in the central nervous system, because spike-timing dependent plasticity (Caporale and Dan, 2008), coincidence detection (Softky, 1994), and the neuronal rhythms of cell ensembles (Buzsáki et al., 2013) precisely tune the arrival times of action potentials.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data on conduction velocity changes and citations to literature on spike-timing dependent processes.

claims.claim: The cerebellum is involved in the accurate control of muscle contraction with a temporal precision of 1–100 ms.
claims.source: The cerebellum is involved in the accurate control of muscle contraction with a temporal precision of 1–100 ms (Hore et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Submillisecond correlations in spike timing occurring between neighboring Purkinje cells have been noted previously.
claims.source: Submillisecond correlations in spike timing occurring between neighboring Purkinje cells have been noted previously (reviewed in Isope et al., 2002; Person and Raman, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Submillisecond precision of the mossy or parallel fiber input are critical for information processing in the cerebellar circuits.
claims.source: Furthermore, submillisecond precision of the mossy or parallel fiber input are critical for information processing in the cerebellar circuits (Braitenberg et al., 1997; Heck et al., 2001; Isope et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The here-described changes in action potential conduction velocity in mossy and parallel fibers may play an important role in cerebellar computation.
claims.source: Together, the here-described changes in action potential conduction velocity in mossy and parallel fibers (Figures 1–3) may thus play an important role in cerebellar computation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data and literature on cerebellar function.

claims.claim: The view of the axon as a cable-like compartment in which conduction velocity is static has substantially changed over recent years in favor of a model that allows flexibility and complex forms of axonal computation.
claims.source: Indeed, the view of the axon as a cable-like compartment in which conduction velocity is static has substantially changed over recent years in favor of a model that allows flexibility and complex forms of axonal computation (Debanne et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Axon diameters change during long-term potentiation.
claims.source: Recent findings showed that axon diameters change during long-term potentiation (Chéreau et al., 2017), and changes in myelination in the motor cortex were resolved during the learning of complex motor skills (McKenzie et al., 2014; for environmental effects on myelination see also Forbes and Gallo, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Changes in myelination in the motor cortex were resolved during the learning of complex motor skills.
claims.source: Recent findings showed that axon diameters change during long-term potentiation (Chéreau et al., 2017), and changes in myelination in the motor cortex were resolved during the learning of complex motor skills (McKenzie et al., 2014; for environmental effects on myelination see also Forbes and Gallo, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The control of conduction velocity is solely mediated by changes in resting membrane potential.
claims.source: Our analysis revealed that the control of conduction velocity is solely mediated by changes in resting membrane potential.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing that only the Vm-model but not the Rm-model affects conduction velocity.

claims.claim: Isolated changes in membrane conductance and thus in the membrane time and length constant had no effect on conduction velocity.
claims.source: Isolated changes in membrane conductance and thus in the membrane time and length constant had no effect on conduction velocity (Figure 9E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling showing that the Rm-model does not affect conduction velocity, as shown in Figure 9E.

claims.claim: The increased conduction velocity upon depolarization is consistent with a previously observed correlation between conduction velocity and the depolarization from the resting potential required to reach the firing threshold in motoneurons.

results.result: HCN channels bidirectionally control action potential conduction velocity in both myelinated and unmyelinated central axons. ZD7288 (30 µM) decreased conduction velocity by 4-9% in mossy fibers, parallel fibers, and optic nerves, while 8-Br-cAMP (500 µM) increased velocity by 4-6% in the same fiber types.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C5-C7 provide consistent experimental evidence across three different axon types showing bidirectional modulation of conduction velocity by HCN channel blocker and cAMP analog. The data include appropriate sample sizes (n=4-17), statistical testing (referenced in Figure 1), and control for potential off-target effects of ZD7288 on Na+ channels (C4). The conclusion (C8) is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple preparations.

results.result: ZD7288 at 30 µM does not affect voltage-dependent Na+ currents in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons.
results.evaluation: Claim C4 is supported by direct recordings from 53 cMFBs showing no change in Na+ current amplitude or kinetics after ZD7288 application (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This control experiment is critical for ruling out off-target effects that could confound interpretation of conduction velocity changes.

results.result: Physiological neuromodulators bidirectionally modulate conduction velocity in cerebellar parallel fibers. Norepinephrine (200 µM) increased velocity by 1.9±0.8%, while serotonin, dopamine, and adenosine (all 200 µM) decreased velocity by 3.5-7.2%.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C12 provide experimental data on neuromodulator effects with appropriate sample sizes (n=5-13). However, the authors acknowledge that high concentrations were used and off-target effects cannot be excluded (C104). The mechanistic link to cAMP-HCN pathway is inferred from receptor pharmacology rather than directly demonstrated. Statistical significance is referenced but specific p-values are not provided in the text for all comparisons.

results.result: The effects of cAMP and neuromodulators on conduction velocity are mainly mediated by HCN channels.
results.evaluation: Claim C14 is supported by experiments (Figure 2F-G) showing that when HCN channels are blocked with ZD7288, neuromodulators no longer affect conduction velocity. The control experiment with ZD7288 alone shows similar decreases to those with ZD7288 plus neuromodulators, indicating HCN channels are the primary mediator. However, the authors appropriately acknowledge that other mechanisms could contribute (C103).

results.result: Cerebellar mossy fiber boutons exhibit a substantial voltage sag (sag ratio 0.497±0.030 at ~-150 mV, n=12) in response to hyperpolarizing current injections, indicating presence of Ih.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 are supported by current-clamp recordings from cMFBs (Figure 3B-C). The voltage sag is a well-established hallmark of HCN channel activity, and the quantification provides appropriate sample size and measurement precision.

results.result: HCN channels do not profoundly alter active membrane properties of cerebellar mossy fiber boutons at low firing frequencies (1 Hz).
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 are supported by measurements showing no significant effect of ZD7288 on action potential amplitude and half-duration at 1 Hz (Figure 4B-C). This establishes that HCN channels primarily affect passive rather than active properties at low frequencies, setting up the contrast with high-frequency effects.

results.result: HCN channels ensure reliable high-frequency firing in cerebellar mossy fibers. Blocking HCN channels reduced the average failure-free frequency from 854±60 Hz to 426±63 Hz (n=20 and 10, p=0.0002).
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 are strongly supported by experimental data (Figure 4D-E) showing significant reduction in maximal failure-free firing frequency with ZD7288. The effect is statistically significant with appropriate sample sizes. Additional data on action potential broadening and amplitude reduction during trains provide mechanistic insight. This is a key functional consequence of HCN channel activity.

results.result: HCN channels determine passive membrane properties of cerebellar mossy fiber boutons in a cAMP-dependent manner. ZD7288 hyperpolarized resting potential by 5.4 mV and doubled input resistance and membrane time constant. Adding cAMP produced opposite, concentration-dependent effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are well-supported by systematic measurements (Figure 5) with large sample sizes (n=35-94 for ZD7288 groups, varying n for cAMP concentrations). The bidirectional effects of HCN blockade versus cAMP application provide strong evidence for cAMP-dependent modulation. Statistical testing is referenced (PANOVA and PKruskal-Wallis <10^-10).

results.result: HCN2 is the dominant subunit in cerebellar mossy fibers, uniformly distributed along the plasma membrane at a density of 22.7±2.4 particles/µm² (n=6 cMFBs). HCN1 showed only background immunoreactivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C34 are supported by immunogold electron microscopy (Figure 6) with quantitative analysis. The identification of HCN2 as the dominant subunit is consistent with the observed strong cAMP-dependence. The uniform distribution without spatial clustering near synapses is clearly documented. Sample size (n=6 cMFBs from 2 mice) is modest but appropriate for EM studies.

results.result: Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons has a V½ of -103.3±0.8 mV (n=36), with approximately 7% of HCN2-mediated current active at rest.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 are supported by voltage-clamp recordings (Figure 7A-B) with large sample size (n=36 independent cMFBs). The calculation that ~7% of current is active at rest (C37) is a straightforward inference from the V½ and average resting potential. This provides important quantitative characterization of HCN channel function.

results.result: Intracellular cAMP shifts Ih activation with an EC50 of 40.4 µM. With 1 mM cAMP, V½ shifted by 17 mV to -86.6±1.2 mV (n=16, p<10^-10).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by systematic voltage-clamp recordings with varying cAMP concentrations (Figure 7B, D). The EC50 determination is based on multiple concentrations with appropriate sample sizes. The large voltage shift with 1 mM cAMP is highly significant statistically.

results.result: The endogenous cAMP concentration in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons is 12.6 µM (68% confidence interval: 1.8-60.7 µM), estimated from perforated patch recordings showing V½ of -96.4±1.2 mV versus -101.3±1.0 mV after patch rupture (n=10, p=0.0076).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 are supported by technically challenging perforated patch recordings (Figure 7C-D). The approach is sound: comparing V½ under perforated patch (preserving endogenous cAMP) versus whole-cell conditions. The 4.9 mV shift is statistically significant. The wide confidence interval (1.8-60.7 µM) reflects uncertainty in the estimation but the central estimate of 12.6 µM is reasonable. The authors appropriately note this may be an underestimate due to higher access resistance in perforated patch.

results.result: The reversal potential of Ih in cerebellar mossy fiber boutons is -23.4±1.4 mV (n=7).
results.evaluation: Claim C42 is supported by voltage ramp measurements (Figure 8C) and is consistent with previous estimates from other preparations. This parameter is essential for computational modeling.

results.result: HCN2 channels control conduction velocity primarily through membrane depolarization rather than changes in membrane conductance. Computational modeling shows that only the Vm-model (simulating depolarization) but not the Rm-model (simulating conductance changes) reproduces experimental effects on conduction velocity.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 and C84-C85 are supported by systematic computational modeling (Figure 9E). The dissection of depolarization versus conductance effects through separate models is elegant and provides clear mechanistic insight. The finding that depolarization increases velocity despite decreasing Na+ channel availability (C44, Figure 9—figure supplement 1) is counterintuitive but well-explained by cable theory. The modeling approach is appropriate and conclusions are well-supported.

results.result: HCN channels incur significant metabolic costs. Maintaining resting potential with Ih is ~100% more expensive than without Ih, ~3-fold more expensive than generating one action potential, and increases total energy requirements by ~30% at physiological firing rates (4 Hz).
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 and C92 are supported by computational modeling of ATP consumption (Figure 9F). The calculations are based on established methods for estimating metabolic costs from ion fluxes. The assumption of 4 Hz average firing rate in vivo (C49) is supported by citations. The conclusion that HCN channels are metabolically expensive is well-justified, though the exact values depend on model parameters.

results.result: HCN channels increase action potential velocity and fidelity in central axons, control velocity primarily by altering resting membrane potential, and are associated with significant metabolic costs.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 represent the main conclusions of the paper, integrating experimental and computational findings. These are well-supported by the collective evidence from conduction velocity measurements (C1-C8), high-frequency firing experiments (C19-C21), and computational modeling (C43-C50). The conclusions are appropriately qualified and acknowledge limitations.

results.result: The cAMP-HCN pathway provides neuromodulators with an opportunity to finely tune energy consumption and temporal delays across axons in the brain.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 is a speculative conclusion that extends beyond the direct experimental evidence. While supported by the demonstrated effects of neuromodulators on conduction velocity (C9-C14) and the metabolic cost calculations (C47-C50), the broader implications for brain function are inferred rather than demonstrated. The claim is reasonable but would require additional in vivo evidence to be fully supported.

results.result: Although HCN-mediated changes in conduction velocity are relatively small (~5%), they can produce significant temporal delays (e.g., 0.5 ms in 3 mm parallel fibers) that may influence spike-timing dependent processes in the CNS.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by experimental data (C74) and reasonable extrapolations based on axon length and velocity from literature (C75). The functional significance (C76) is inferred from citations to literature on spike-timing dependent plasticity and coincidence detection. The reasoning is sound though the in vivo relevance remains to be demonstrated.

results.result: The modeling results showing increased conduction velocity with depolarization are consistent with previous observations in motoneurons and with nonlinear cable theory predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 appropriately contextualize the modeling results within prior literature. The consistency with cable theory (Jack et al. 1983) and previous experimental observations (Carp et al. 2003) strengthens confidence in the modeling conclusions.

results.result: HCN channels ensure reliable high-frequency firing by counteracting hyperpolarization during high-frequency trains.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 integrate experimental findings (C19-C21) with mechanistic interpretation supported by literature (Waxman et al. 1995). The explanation is consistent with the observed effects on firing frequency and action potential properties during trains.

results.result: A metabolically cheaper way to depolarize the membrane would be expression of fewer Na+-K+-ATPases, resulting in a depolarized K+ reversal potential.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 is speculative and based on theoretical considerations from the Vm-model. While logically sound, the authors acknowledge this alternative design might complicate high-frequency firing. This represents a thoughtful discussion point rather than a tested hypothesis.

results.result: The estimated endogenous cAMP concentration (12.6 µM) is higher than previous estimates in other systems, though high concentrations may be limited to spatially restricted domains. This high concentration and HCN2 expression facilitate bidirectional neuromodulator control.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C98 appropriately contextualize the cAMP concentration estimate (C41) within prior literature. The comparison to other systems (C94) is factual. The acknowledgment of possible spatial compartmentalization (C96-C97) is appropriately cautious. The functional interpretation (C98) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: Changes in action potential conduction velocity in mossy and parallel fibers may play an important role in cerebellar computation.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is speculative, extending experimental findings to functional significance in cerebellar circuits. While the reasoning is supported by citations to literature on cerebellar timing precision (C77-C79), direct evidence for the role of HCN-mediated velocity changes in cerebellar computation is lacking.

results.result: The cAMP-HCN pathway in axons could contribute to reduced energy consumption of the brain during sleep.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is highly speculative, connecting the metabolic cost findings (C47-C50) and neuromodulator effects (C100-C101) to sleep physiology. While the hypothesis is interesting and supported by citations, it lacks direct experimental evidence and represents a suggestion for future investigation.

results.result: Other mechanisms beyond HCN channels could contribute to neuromodulation of conduction velocity, and off-target interactions cannot be excluded with the concentrations of neuromodulators used.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 represent appropriate acknowledgment of limitations. The authors correctly note that while HCN channels are the main mediator (C14), other voltage-gated channels could contribute, and the high neuromodulator concentrations used may have off-target effects. This demonstrates scientific rigor.

results.result: HCN channels could play a compensatory role in restoring conduction velocity in some diseases.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is speculative, suggesting a potential clinical relevance based on the experimental findings. While the hypothesis is reasonable given the documented role of HCN channels in various pathologies (C106), direct evidence for compensatory function is lacking.
